title: Timing, Nerve Selection, and Restoration Across the Spectrum of Facial Nerve Palsy
content: Background Facial palsy spans a spectrum from acute denervation to chronic paralysis and synkinesis, yet management remains largely technique-driven rather than guided by underlying denervation biology and donor nerve physiology. Optimal reconstructive decision-making depends on timing of denervation, motor endplate viability, axonal input, and cortical adaptability. A unified framework integrating these variables across stages of paralysis is lacking. Methods A narrative review was performed synthesizing current microsurgical techniques in facial reanimation, including primary neurorrhaphy, interposition grafting, nerve transfers, cross-facial nerve grafting (CFNG), free functional muscle transfer (FFMT), regional muscle transposition, and selective neurectomy. These modalities were organized into a physiology-driven algorithm based on denervation timing and donor nerve characteristics. Results Facial palsy can be conceptualized into four clinical states: (1) acute denervation, where early repair or grafting preserves native musculature; (2) subacute paralysis, where nerve transfers and CFNG optimize reinnervation while motor endplates remain viable; (3) chronic denervation, where irreversible muscle loss necessitates FFMT or regional muscle transfer; and (4) synkinesis-dominant recovery, managed with staged neuromodulation and selective neurectomy. Donor nerve selection is guided by tradeoffs between axonal load, spontaneity, and morbidity. Integration of standardized outcome measures, including validated grading systems and objective symmetry analysis, is essential for meaningful comparison across techniques. Conclusions A timing- and donor nerve-based microsurgical algorithm provides a physiology-driven framework for facial reanimation. Aligning reconstructive strategy with denervation biology may improve decision-making, enhance consistency, and support more rigorous outcome evaluation across the spectrum of facial palsy.
